definition: A columnar, analytics-optimized store for querying large volumes of integrated historical data.
explanation: A data warehouse (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift) is built for OLAP: scan billions of rows, aggregate, and join for reporting. It separates analytics from the transactional apps that feed it.
interviewLine: A warehouse is a columnar OLAP store optimized to scan and aggregate large historical datasets, kept separate from OLTP systems.
whyItMatters: It's the destination of most data pipelines and where BI actually runs.

definition: Storing data column-by-column instead of row-by-row, so analytic scans read only needed columns.
explanation: A query touching 3 of 200 columns reads only those 3. Same-type values stored together compress far better and vectorize on CPU. The tradeoff: single-row inserts/updates are expensive — hence OLAP not OLTP.
interviewLine: Columnar storage reads only the columns a query needs and compresses same-type data hard, making big aggregations fast.
whyItMatters: Columnar layout is THE reason warehouses scan huge tables fast — the top warehouse interview point.
interviewQuestion: Why is columnar great for analytics but bad for OLTP updates?

definition: Massively Parallel Processing: split a query across many nodes that each work on a data slice, then combine.
explanation: A warehouse shards data across nodes; a query runs in parallel on all of them and a coordinator merges results. Doubling nodes roughly halves scan time — scale-out, not a bigger single box.
interviewLine: MPP runs one query across many nodes in parallel, each on a data slice, then merges — scale-out throughput for big scans.
whyItMatters: MPP is how warehouses stay fast as data grows into the terabytes.
commonMistake: Assuming more nodes always helps — skewed data or heavy shuffles leave one node the bottleneck.

definition: The cloud-warehouse shift: data lives in cheap object storage; compute clusters spin up independently on top.
explanation: Classic warehouses tied storage to compute nodes. Snowflake/BigQuery decouple them — store once in S3/GCS, run many independent compute clusters that scale up/down and pause, each reading the same data.
interviewLine: Separating storage from compute lets you scale or pause query clusters independently of the data, sizing each to its workload.
whyItMatters: It's why you can scale a heavy query without resizing storage, and pay only for compute you use.
interviewQuestion: How does decoupling storage and compute change how you handle a concurrency spike?

definition: Three layers: cloud storage, independent 'virtual warehouses' (compute), and a cloud services brain.
explanation: Data sits in object storage as micro-partitions. Virtual warehouses are compute clusters you size (XS–6XL) per workload, isolated from each other. The services layer handles metadata, optimization, and security.
interviewLine: Snowflake splits storage, per-workload virtual warehouses, and a services layer, so teams get isolated compute over one copy of data.
whyItMatters: Virtual warehouses give each team isolated compute over shared data — no more noisy-neighbor contention.

definition: Serverless: Dremel executes queries on ephemeral 'slots', reading from Colossus storage over the Jupiter network.
explanation: No clusters to manage. BigQuery allocates slots (units of compute) on demand, Dremel builds a tree of workers, and the fast Jupiter network lets compute read Colossus storage as if local. You pay per bytes scanned or per slot.
interviewLine: BigQuery is serverless: Dremel runs queries on on-demand slots reading Colossus storage, so cost tracks bytes scanned, not clusters.
whyItMatters: Fully serverless means no sizing — but 'bytes scanned' billing makes partitioning and column selection matter a lot.
commonMistake: SELECT * on a huge table — you're billed for every byte scanned, not the rows returned.

definition: A leader node plans queries; compute nodes split into slices that each process a data partition in parallel.
explanation: Redshift is classic MPP: the leader node compiles a plan and distributes it; compute nodes (and their slices) scan their share. Classic Redshift ties storage to nodes; RA3 adds managed storage to decouple them.
interviewLine: Redshift's leader node plans and compute-node slices execute in parallel; performance hinges on distribution and sort keys.
whyItMatters: Its node/slice model is why distribution and sort keys make or break Redshift performance.

definition: How rows are spread across nodes; a good key co-locates joined rows so the join needs no data shuffle.
explanation: Distribute two large tables on their join key and matching rows land on the same node — the join runs locally. Wrong key forces a broadcast/shuffle across the network, the top cause of slow MPP joins.
interviewLine: Distribution keys place rows on nodes; matching the join key co-locates rows so joins avoid a network shuffle.
whyItMatters: Co-locating joins by distribution key is the highest-leverage Redshift tuning move.
interviewQuestion: Why can the wrong distribution key make a two-table join collapse to one node?

definition: Physically ordering data by a column so the engine skips blocks that can't match a filter (pruning).
explanation: Sort/cluster on the column you filter most (often a date). The engine keeps min/max per block and reads only blocks in range — turning a full scan into a targeted one. Snowflake auto-clusters; Redshift uses sort keys.
interviewLine: Sort/cluster keys order data so the engine prunes blocks outside a filter's range, scanning far less.
whyItMatters: Sorting by your filter column is the difference between scanning a day and scanning a year.

definition: Snowflake's automatic small storage units, each with min/max metadata that enables pruning without manual partitioning.
explanation: Snowflake auto-splits tables into ~compressed micro-partitions and records each one's column ranges. A filtered query reads only micro-partitions whose range overlaps — pruning you get for free, tunable via clustering.
interviewLine: Micro-partitions are Snowflake's auto storage units with min/max metadata, so queries prune irrelevant partitions with no manual setup.
whyItMatters: It's why Snowflake needs no manual partition scheme yet still prunes big scans.

definition: A view whose results are precomputed and stored, refreshed on change, so repeat queries are instant.
explanation: A regular view re-runs its SQL every time; a materialized view stores the answer and incrementally refreshes as base data changes. Great for expensive aggregations hit by many dashboards.
interviewLine: A materialized view stores precomputed results and auto-refreshes, so repeated expensive aggregations return instantly.
whyItMatters: It trades storage and refresh cost for near-instant reads of expensive rollups.
commonMistake: Materializing a query over rapidly-changing data — constant refresh can cost more than it saves.

definition: Columnar data compresses hard because each column holds one data type with repeating values.
explanation: Encodings like run-length, dictionary, and delta shrink columns dramatically — a low-cardinality column can compress 10x+. Less data on disk means less I/O, which is the main cost of a scan.
interviewLine: Columnar compression (dictionary, run-length, delta) shrinks storage and, more importantly, the I/O a scan must read.
whyItMatters: Compression cuts both storage bill and scan time — the two things warehouses charge for.

definition: Physically splitting a table by a column (usually date) so queries scan only relevant partitions.
explanation: Partition a big events table by day; a query for last week reads 7 partitions, not the whole table. In BigQuery this directly cuts bytes scanned (and cost); it also makes dropping old data a partition drop.
interviewLine: Partitioning splits a table by a key like date so queries prune to a few partitions, cutting scan time and (in BigQuery) cost.
whyItMatters: Partition + cluster on the right columns is the main lever on both speed and BigQuery cost.
interviewQuestion: How do partitioning and clustering combine to reduce bytes scanned?

definition: Cloud warehouses bill for compute time (Snowflake credits) or bytes scanned (BigQuery) — the FinOps angle.
explanation: Snowflake charges per-second while a virtual warehouse runs, so auto-suspend and right-sizing matter. BigQuery on-demand charges per byte scanned, so partitioning, clustering, and avoiding SELECT * are the cost levers.
interviewLine: Snowflake bills compute-seconds (auto-suspend, right-size); BigQuery bills bytes scanned (partition, cluster, no SELECT *).
whyItMatters: Warehouse bills spiral without these habits; cost-awareness is an increasingly asked skill.
commonMistake: Leaving a large virtual warehouse running idle, or scanning full tables when a filter would prune them.
